decks.title: Ray Optics — Part 1: Mirrors, refraction and total internal reflection
goals: Apply the mirror formula and magnification with the New Cartesian sign convention
Use Snell’s law and the refractive index
Explain total internal reflection, the critical angle and optical fibres

slides.heading: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
slides.body_md: Part 1 — light as rays: images in curved mirrors, bending at boundaries, and light trapped inside glass by total internal reflection.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: spherical mirrors, mirror formula, Snell’s law, total internal reflection, optical fibres

slides.narration: Ray optics treats light as rays that travel in straight lines and bend at boundaries. It explains a car’s rear-view mirror, the sparkle of a diamond and the internet signals racing through glass fibres under the sea. In this part we revisit curved mirrors with the mirror formula, then study refraction and the special case of total internal reflection.

slides.heading: Mirror formula and magnification
slides.body_md:
With the **New Cartesian sign convention** (distances from the pole; along the incident light positive; heights up positive):
$$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f},\qquad f = \dfrac{R}{2},\qquad m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = -\dfrac{v}{u}$$
Concave mirror: $f < 0$. Convex mirror: $f > 0$. Real images: $v < 0$ and $m < 0$.

slides.narration: Measure all distances from the pole of the mirror. Distances in the direction of the incident light are positive, and those against it are negative, so for a real object u is negative. The mirror formula links u, v and f, and the focal length is half the radius of curvature. A negative magnification means an inverted image. This ray diagram is computed directly from the formula.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a concave mirror
slides.body_md: An object is 25 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position, nature and magnification of the image.
bullets: Step 1 — signs: $u = -25$ cm, $f = -15$ cm.
Step 2 — $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{25} = -\dfrac{2}{75}$, so $v = -37.5$ cm.
Step 3 — $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-37.5}{-25} = -1.5$: real, inverted, 1.5 times enlarged, 37.5 cm in front of the mirror.

The formula gives v equals minus thirty seven point five centimetres, so the image is in front of the mirror and real. slides.heading: Convex mirrors
slides.body_md: A convex mirror always forms a **virtual, erect, diminished** image behind it, whatever the object distance; it gives a wide field of view (rear-view mirrors, shop security mirrors).

With an object thirty centimetres in front and a focal length of twenty, the image forms twelve centimetres behind the mirror, erect and only zero point four times as tall. That reduced, upright and wide view is exactly what a driver needs in a rear-view mirror.

slides.heading: Refraction and Snell’s law
slides.body_md: At a boundary, $n_1\sin i = n_2\sin r$. The **refractive index** of a medium is $n = c/v$. Light bends **towards** the normal entering a denser medium and away from it leaving.
bullets: Relative index $n_{21} = n_2/n_1 = v_1/v_2$.
Apparent depth: an object under water looks nearer: apparent depth = real depth / n (for near-normal viewing).
Frequency is unchanged; wavelength and speed change.

visual.alt: Table of refractive indices and speeds of light in air, water, glass and diamond

slides.narration: When light crosses into another medium its speed changes, so it bends. Snell’s law says n one sine i equals n two sine r. The refractive index n is the speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in the medium. Going into a denser medium the ray bends towards the normal. A swimming pool looks shallower than it is because rays from the bottom bend away from the normal as they leave the water.

slides.heading: Total internal reflection
slides.body_md:
Going from a denser to a rarer medium, the refracted ray bends away from the normal. At the **critical angle** $C$ it grazes the surface ($r = 90^\circ$):
$$\sin C = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\quad(\text{into air: } \sin C = 1/n)$$
For $i > C$ there is no refracted ray: all the light is reflected — **total internal reflection** (TIR).
bullets: Conditions: light goes from denser to rarer, and i > C.

slides.narration: Shine light from water up into air at increasing angles. At first it refracts out, bending away from the normal. At one angle, the critical angle, the refracted ray just skims along the surface. Beyond that, no light gets out at all: the surface acts as a perfect mirror. This is total internal reflection. It needs light travelling from the denser medium and an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: critical angles
slides.body_md: Find the critical angle for light going from (a) glass (n = 1.5), (b) water (n = 1.33), (c) diamond (n = 2.42) into air.
bullets: (a) $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{1.5}$: $C \approx 41.8^\circ$.
(b) $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{1.33}$: $C \approx 48.8^\circ$.
(c) $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{2.42}$: $C \approx 24.4^\circ$ — very small, so light entering a cut diamond is totally reflected many times and the stone sparkles.

visual.alt: Worked table: critical angles of about 41.8 degrees for glass, 48.8 degrees for water and 24.4 degrees for diamond

slides.narration: Take the inverse sine of one over n in each case. Glass gives about forty two degrees, water about forty nine degrees and diamond only about twenty four degrees. Because a diamond’s critical angle is so small, light that enters a well-cut stone is reflected again and again inside before escaping through the top facets, which is why it sparkles.

slides.heading: Optical fibres
slides.body_md: A thin glass **core** is surrounded by **cladding** of lower refractive index. Light entering the core meets the boundary at more than the critical angle and is totally reflected again and again, travelling far with little loss.
bullets: Uses: internet and telephone links, endoscopes for seeing inside the body, decorative lamps.
Other TIR examples: mirages on hot roads, totally reflecting prisms in periscopes and binoculars, the sparkle of diamonds.

slides.narration: An optical fibre is a hair-thin strand of very pure glass with a core and a cladding of slightly lower refractive index. Light inside the core strikes the boundary at a large angle, beyond the critical angle, so it is totally reflected each time and zigzags along the fibre for kilometres. Fibres carry internet data under the oceans, and bundles of them let doctors see inside the body.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the core–cladding boundary
slides.body_md: An optical fibre has a core of index 1.50 and cladding of index 1.45. Find the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary.
bullets: Step 1 — $\sin C = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{1.45}{1.50} \approx 0.967$.
Step 2 — $C \approx 75.2^\circ$.
Meaning — light must strike the wall at more than about 75° to the normal, i.e. travel nearly along the fibre, to be guided.

slides.narration: At the core–cladding boundary the light goes from index one point five to index one point four five, so sine C is their ratio, about zero point nine six seven, and C is about seventy five degrees. Only rays travelling nearly parallel to the fibre’s axis meet the wall at more than this angle and are trapped. That is why light must be fed in close to the axis.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

visual.alt: Summary table of the mirror formula, magnification, Snell’s law, the critical angle and conditions for total internal reflection

slides.narration: To sum up: use the sign convention with the mirror formula, one over v plus one over u equals one over f, and magnification minus v over u. Refraction follows Snell’s law, with the refractive index equal to c over v. Light going from a denser to a rarer medium at more than the critical angle is totally reflected; optical fibres, diamonds and periscope prisms all use this.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Write the sign of every quantity before substituting; a sign error flips the answer.
State both conditions for TIR in every answer.
In fibre questions, the critical angle is at the core–cladding boundary: $\sin C = n_\text{cladding}/n_\text{core}$.
Draw ray diagrams with arrows, and dashed lines for virtual rays and images.

visual.alt: Table of the sign of f and the kind of image for concave and convex mirrors

slides.narration: Most marks are lost on signs, so write each quantity with its sign before using a formula. When explaining total internal reflection, always give both conditions. For optical fibres, remember that the relevant boundary is between core and cladding. And in ray diagrams, use arrows on rays and dashed lines for anything virtual.

goals: Derive refraction at a spherical surface and the lens maker’s formula

slides.heading: Spherical surfaces, lenses and the prism
slides.body_md: Part 2 — from one curved surface to a thin lens, combinations of lenses, and the prism.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: refraction at one spherical surface, lens maker’s formula, thin lens formula, power and combinations, prism

slides.narration: A lens is just two curved refracting surfaces close together. In this part we first find how one curved surface forms an image, then apply it twice to get the lens maker’s formula and the thin lens formula. We define the power of a lens, combine lenses, and finally see how a prism deviates light, with a minimum deviation that lets us measure refractive index.

slides.heading: Refraction at a spherical surface
slides.body_md:
For a point object in medium $n_1$ and a spherical surface of radius $R$ bounding medium $n_2$ (paraxial rays, sign convention from the pole):
$$\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$$
bullets: Derivation: apply Snell’s law (small angles) at the point where a ray meets the surface, and relate the angles to u, v and R.

slides.heading: The lens maker’s formula
slides.body_md:
Apply the spherical-surface result to the first surface (image $I_1$), then use $I_1$ as the object for the second surface. For a thin lens of index $n$ in air:
$$\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$$
bullets: Biconvex: $R_1 > 0$, $R_2 < 0$, so $f > 0$ (converging).
In a medium of index $n_m$, replace $n$ by $n/n_m$: a lens can even become diverging in a denser liquid.

slides.heading: Thin lens formula and magnification
slides.body_md:
$$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f},\qquad m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = \dfrac{v}{u}$$
Convex lens: $f > 0$; concave lens: $f < 0$. A real image has $v > 0$ and $m < 0$.

slides.heading: Power of a lens; lenses in contact
slides.body_md:
**Power** $P = \dfrac{1}{f}$ (f in metres); unit **dioptre** (D = m$^{-1}$). Converging: $P > 0$; diverging: $P < 0$.
Thin lenses in contact: $\dfrac{1}{F} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2}$, i.e. $P = P_1 + P_2$; magnifications multiply: $m = m_1m_2$.

visual.alt: Table of the powers of a 50 centimetre convex lens, a 25 centimetre concave lens and the two in contact

slides.narration: The power of a lens is one over its focal length in metres, measured in dioptres. A strong lens has a short focal length and a large power. Converging lenses have positive power and diverging lenses negative. For thin lenses in contact, powers simply add, which is how opticians combine lenses. The total magnification is the product of the separate magnifications.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: combining lenses
slides.body_md: A convex lens of power +5.0 D is placed in contact with a concave lens of power −2.0 D. Find the power and focal length of the combination. Is it converging or diverging?
bullets: Step 2 — $F = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{3.0} \approx 0.333$ m $= 33.3$ cm.
Step 3 — positive power: the combination is **converging**.

visual.alt: Worked table: plus five dioptres and minus two dioptres combine to plus three dioptres, a focal length of about 33 centimetres

slides.narration: Add the powers: five minus two gives plus three dioptres. The focal length is one third of a metre, about thirty three centimetres. Because the total power is positive, the pair behaves as a converging lens, weaker than the convex lens alone. Combining lenses this way is used in camera lenses and spectacles.

slides.heading: Refraction through a prism
slides.body_md:
For a prism of angle A: $r_1 + r_2 = A$ and the deviation is $\delta = i + e - A$. At **minimum deviation** $i = e$ and $r_1 = r_2 = A/2$, so
$$n = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}$$

slides.heading: Worked example 8: refractive index from δm
slides.body_md: A prism of angle 60° gives a minimum deviation of 30°. Find the refractive index of its glass.
bullets: Step 1 — $\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2} = \dfrac{60 + 30}{2} = 45^\circ$; $\dfrac{A}{2} = 30^\circ$.
Step 2 — $n = \dfrac{\sin 45^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} = \dfrac{0.707}{0.5} \approx 1.41$.
Check — the angle of incidence at minimum deviation is 45°.

slides.body_md: Key results:

visual.alt: Summary table of refraction at a spherical surface, the lens maker’s formula, the thin lens formula, power and the prism relations

slides.narration: To sum up: one curved surface obeys n two over v minus n one over u equals n two minus n one over R. Applying it twice gives the lens maker’s formula. goals: Derive the magnifying power of a simple microscope

slides.heading: Optical instruments
slides.body_md: Part 3 — using lenses and mirrors to see the very small and the very far.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: simple microscope, compound microscope, refracting telescope, reflecting telescope

slides.narration: Our eyes cannot see bacteria or the moons of Jupiter, because they look too small: they make too small an angle at the eye. Optical instruments increase that angle. In this part we see how a single magnifying glass works, how two lenses make a compound microscope, and how telescopes, both refracting and reflecting, bring distant objects closer.

slides.heading: Magnifying power and the simple microscope
slides.body_md:
**Magnifying power** $m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}$: angle subtended at the eye by the image ÷ angle subtended by the object at the near point ($D = 25$ cm). For a convex lens of focal length $f$ held close to the eye:
$$m = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f}\ \ (\text{image at } D),\qquad m = \dfrac{D}{f}\ \ (\text{image at infinity, relaxed eye})$$

visual.alt: Table of the magnifying power of a simple microscope for an image at the near point and at infinity

slides.narration: What matters is the angle an object makes at the eye. Without help, the largest angle comes from holding the object at the near point, about twenty five centimetres. A convex lens lets you bring the object much closer and still see it clearly. The magnifying power is one plus D over f when the image is at the near point, and D over f when it is at infinity, which is more comfortable.

slides.heading: Worked example 9: a magnifying glass
slides.body_md: A jeweller uses a convex lens of focal length 5.0 cm as a simple microscope. Find its magnifying power when the image is (a) at the near point, (b) at infinity.
bullets: Note — a shorter focal length gives a larger magnification.

visual.alt: Worked table: magnifying power 6 with the image at the near point and 5 with the image at infinity

slides.narration: With a five centimetre lens, D over f is five. If the jeweller places the image at the near point, the magnification is one more, six. With a relaxed eye, viewing the image at infinity, it is five. A stronger lens, with a shorter focal length, would magnify more, but very short focal lengths cause blurred images, which is why compound microscopes are used for higher magnification.

slides.heading: The compound microscope
slides.body_md:
The **objective** (short focal length $f_o$) forms a real, inverted, enlarged image of the object; the **eyepiece** (focal length $f_e$) magnifies this image like a simple microscope.
$$m = m_o m_e \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)\ \text{(final image at } D),\qquad m \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e}\ \text{(at infinity)}$$
$L$ is the tube length (distance between the second focus of the objective and the first focus of the eyepiece).

slides.narration: A compound microscope uses two converging lenses. The objective, with a very short focal length, forms a real, inverted and enlarged image inside the tube. The eyepiece then acts as a magnifying glass on that image, producing a large virtual final image. The total magnification is the product of the two: roughly L over f o, times D over f e when the final image is at infinity.

slides.heading: Worked example 10: a school microscope
slides.body_md: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 1.0 cm, an eyepiece of focal length 5.0 cm and a tube length of 15 cm. Estimate its magnifying power in normal adjustment (final image at infinity).
bullets: Step 1 — objective: $m_o \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o} = \dfrac{15}{1.0} = 15$.
Step 2 — eyepiece: $m_e = \dfrac{D}{f_e} = \dfrac{25}{5.0} = 5$.
Step 3 — $m \approx 15 \times 5 = 75$.

slides.heading: The astronomical (refracting) telescope
slides.body_md:
The **objective** (long focal length $f_o$, large aperture) forms an image of a distant object at its focus; the **eyepiece** (short $f_e$) magnifies it. In **normal adjustment** the final image is at infinity:
$$m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e},\qquad \text{tube length } L = f_o + f_e$$
The final image is inverted (no problem for astronomy).

slides.heading: Reflecting telescopes
slides.body_md: Large telescopes use a **concave mirror** as the objective. In the **Cassegrain** design, a small convex secondary mirror reflects the light back through a hole in the primary to the eyepiece or camera.
bullets: No **chromatic aberration** (mirrors reflect all colours alike).
A **paraboloidal** mirror removes spherical aberration.
A mirror can be supported from behind, so it can be made very large; it is lighter and cheaper than a lens of the same size.

slides.narration: Big research telescopes, such as the two metre telescope at Hanle in Ladakh, use mirrors instead of lenses. Light from the sky falls on a large concave primary mirror, reflects to a small convex secondary, and returns through a hole in the primary to the camera. Mirrors have no colour fringes, can be shaped to avoid spherical aberration, and can be supported from behind, so they can be built very large.

sections.heading: 2. Refraction and total internal reflection
sections.body_md:
**Snell’s law:** $n_1\sin i = n_2\sin r$; $n = c/v$. Towards the normal into a denser medium. Apparent depth = real depth / n (near-normal viewing). Frequency unchanged across a boundary.

**Total internal reflection:** from denser to rarer, at the **critical angle** C the refracted ray grazes the surface: $\sin C = n_2/n_1$ (into air: $1/n$). For $i > C$ all light is reflected. Conditions: denser → rarer **and** i > C.

Critical angles: glass (1.5) ≈ 41.8°, water (1.33) ≈ 48.8°, diamond (2.42) ≈ 24.4°.

**Applications:** optical fibres (core of higher n than cladding; guided by repeated TIR; communication, endoscopy), sparkle of diamonds, totally reflecting prisms (periscopes, binoculars), mirages.

key_terms.definition_md: Angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is 90°.
A glass fibre that guides light by repeated total internal reflection between core and cladding.

sections.heading: 3. Spherical surfaces and lenses
sections.body_md:
**One spherical surface:** $\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$ (paraxial rays).

**Lens maker’s formula** (thin lens of index n in air): $\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$. In a medium of index $n_m$ use $n/n_m$.

**Thin lens formula:** $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$, $m = \dfrac{v}{u}$. Convex f > 0; concave f < 0.

**Power:** $P = 1/f$ (f in m), dioptre (D). Thin lenses in contact: $P = P_1 + P_2 + \dots$, $m = m_1m_2$.

sections.heading: 4. Refraction through a prism
sections.body_md:
For a prism of angle A: $r_1 + r_2 = A$; deviation $\delta = i + e - A$.

As i increases, δ decreases to a minimum $\delta_m$ and then increases. At minimum deviation $i = e$, $r_1 = r_2 = A/2$, the ray inside is parallel to the base, and
$$n = \dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$$
For a 60° prism of n = 1.5: $i = 48.6°$, $\delta_m \approx 37.2°$. (Thin prism: $\delta \approx (n - 1)A$.)

key_terms.definition_md: The smallest deviation produced by a prism, when the ray passes through it symmetrically.

sections.heading: 5. Optical instruments
sections.body_md:
**Magnifying power** = angle subtended at the eye by the image / angle subtended by the object at the near point (D = 25 cm).

- **Simple microscope:** $m = 1 + D/f$ (image at D); $m = D/f$ (image at infinity).
- **Compound microscope:** objective (very short $f_o$) gives a real, inverted, enlarged image just inside the focus of the eyepiece; $m = m_om_e \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e}$ (infinity) or $\dfrac{L}{f_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$ (at D), L = tube length.
- **Astronomical telescope:** long $f_o$, large aperture; normal adjustment $m = f_o/f_e$, tube length $f_o + f_e$; final image inverted.
- **Reflecting telescope (Cassegrain):** concave primary, convex secondary, light through a hole in the primary. Advantages: no chromatic aberration, paraboloidal mirror removes spherical aberration, large mirrors can be supported from behind, cheaper and lighter.

key_terms.definition_md: Ratio of the angle subtended at the eye by the image to that subtended by the object (at the near point for microscopes, directly for telescopes).

questions.stem_md: In the New Cartesian sign convention, with light incident from the left, which is correct?

options.text_md: The focal length of a concave mirror is positive and that of a convex mirror is negative
Both mirrors have positive focal lengths
The sign of f depends on where the object is
The focal length of a concave mirror is negative and that of a convex mirror is positive

questions.solution_md: The focus of a concave mirror is in front (against the incident light); that of a convex mirror is behind — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A candle flame stands 36 cm in front of a concave mirror whose radius of curvature is 48 cm. Where must a screen be placed to catch a sharp image? Give v with its sign, in cm.
questions.solution_md: $f = R/2 = -24$ cm and $u = -36$ cm. $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{24} + \dfrac{1}{36} = -\dfrac{1}{72}$, so $v = -72$ cm: the screen goes 72 cm in front of the mirror (real image).

questions.stem_md: An object is 10 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. The image is

options.text_md: real, inverted and 3 times enlarged, 30 cm in front
virtual, erect and 3 times enlarged, 30 cm behind the mirror
virtual, erect and diminished, 6 cm behind
at infinity

questions.stem_md: An object is 50 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 25 cm. Find the image distance, in cm (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{25} + \dfrac{1}{50} = \dfrac{3}{50}$, so $v = \dfrac{50}{3} = 16.7$ cm (virtual, behind the mirror).

questions.stem_md: A dentist’s or shaving mirror gives an enlarged, upright image of the face or tooth. It is

options.text_md: a convex mirror, with the object anywhere
a concave mirror, with the object beyond its centre of curvature
a concave mirror, with the object inside its focal length
a plane mirror

questions.solution_md: Only a concave mirror with the object between P and F gives a virtual, erect, enlarged image — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Convex mirrors are used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles because they

options.text_md: give an enlarged image of following vehicles
form real images on the windscreen
have no focal point
always give an erect, diminished image and a wide field of view

questions.solution_md: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image, so a wide area fits in a small mirror — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A convex mirror can never form a real image of a real object.

**Reason (R):** For a convex mirror f > 0 and for a real object u < 0, so 1/v = 1/f − 1/u is always positive.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; v > 0 means the image is always behind the mirror (virtual), which R proves — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A concave mirror forms a real image 60 cm in front of it of an object placed 30 cm in front of it. Find the magnitude of its focal length, in cm.
True or false? A plane mirror can be thought of as a spherical mirror of infinite radius of curvature, so its focal length is infinite.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. With R → ∞, f = R/2 → ∞; the mirror formula then gives v = −u (image as far behind as the object is in front).

questions.stem_md: Using the mirror formula, show why a convex mirror always forms a diminished image of a real object.

answer.model_answer_md: For a convex mirror $f > 0$ and $u < 0$, so $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{|u|}$. This is larger than $\dfrac{1}{|u|}$, so $v < |u|$. Then $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{v}{|u|}$ lies between 0 and 1: the image is **erect and diminished** (and virtual, since v > 0).

questions.solution_md: Compare v with |u| from the formula.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Total internal reflection can occur when light passes from air into glass.

**Reason (R):** Glass has a higher refractive index than air.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: TIR needs light travelling from the denser to the rarer medium (glass to air), not air to glass — option (d).

A ray in air strikes glass (n = 1.5) at an angle of incidence of 45°. Find the angle of refraction, in degrees (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\sin r = \dfrac{\sin 45^\circ}{1.5} = \dfrac{0.707}{1.5} \approx 0.471$, so $r = \sin^{-1}(0.471) = 28.1$ degrees.

questions.stem_md: A water tank is 2.0 m deep (n = 1.33). Viewed from directly above, how deep does it appear? Answer in metres (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Apparent depth $= \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{n} = \dfrac{2.0}{1.33} \approx 1.50$ m.

On a hot summer afternoon, a highway in Rajasthan seems to have pools of water on it. This mirage is due to

options.text_md: total internal reflection of light from the sky in the hot, less dense air near the road
reflection of light from oil on the road
diffraction of light by the hot road
dispersion of sunlight

questions.solution_md: Air near the hot road is rarer; light from the sky bending through layers of decreasing index meets one at more than the critical angle and is totally reflected upwards — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A well-cut diamond sparkles much more than a glass imitation of the same shape mainly because diamond has

options.text_md: a much smaller critical angle, so light is totally reflected many times inside
a larger critical angle, so more light escapes
a lower refractive index
a rough surface that scatters light

questions.solution_md: Diamond’s n ≈ 2.42 gives C ≈ 24°; most light striking inner faces is totally reflected before leaving through the top — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In an optical fibre, the refractive index of the core must be

options.text_md: less than that of the cladding
equal to that of the cladding
less than that of air
greater than that of the cladding

questions.solution_md: TIR at the core–cladding boundary needs light going from the denser core to the rarer cladding — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The critical angle for a transparent material in air is 30°. Its refractive index is
questions.solution_md: $n = \dfrac{1}{\sin C} = \dfrac{1}{\sin 30^\circ} = 2$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A right-angled isosceles glass prism is used in binoculars to turn light through 90° by total internal reflection at its hypotenuse face, where the angle of incidence is 45°. This works only if the refractive index of the glass is

options.text_md: less than √2
exactly 1
greater than √2 (about 1.41)
greater than 2

questions.solution_md: TIR needs $45^\circ > C$, i.e. $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n} < \sin 45^\circ$, so $n > \sqrt{2}$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Light travels from glass (n = 1.50) into water (n = 1.33). The critical angle at the glass–water surface is about

options.text_md: There is no critical angle for this pair

questions.solution_md: $\sin C = \dfrac{1.33}{1.50} \approx 0.887$, so $C \approx 62.5^\circ$ — larger than for glass–air because the indices are closer — option (d).

questions.stem_md: What is total internal reflection? State the two conditions needed for it.

answer.model_answer_md: When light travelling in a **denser** medium meets a boundary with a rarer medium at an angle of incidence **greater than the critical angle**, no light is refracted: **all** of it is reflected back into the denser medium. Conditions: (1) light goes from denser to rarer; (2) the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.

questions.solution_md: Definition plus two conditions.

questions.stem_md: Why are right-angled glass prisms, rather than plane mirrors, used to turn light in good periscopes and binoculars?

answer.model_answer_md: At the hypotenuse face the light meets the glass–air boundary at **45°**, more than the critical angle (about 42° for glass), so it is **totally** reflected: **100%** of the light is reflected, with no silvering to tarnish. A plane mirror absorbs some light and its silvering degrades, and a back-silvered mirror gives faint double images.

questions.solution_md: TIR reflects all the light.

marking_scheme.step: Total reflection, brighter, no tarnishing silver

questions.stem_md: An optical fibre has a core of index 1.55 and cladding of index 1.45. (a) Find the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary. (b) A ray inside the core makes 15° with the fibre axis. Will it be guided along the fibre? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\sin C = \dfrac{1.45}{1.55} \approx 0.935$, so $C \approx 69.3^\circ$.
(b) A ray at 15° to the axis meets the wall (parallel to the axis) at an angle of incidence of $90^\circ - 15^\circ = 75^\circ$. This is **more than** the critical angle (about 69.3°), so it is **totally reflected** each time and is guided along the fibre.

questions.solution_md: Find C; angle of incidence = 90° − angle to axis.

An object is 10 cm from a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. Find the image distance v, with its sign, in cm.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{10} = -\dfrac{1}{30}$, so $v = -30$ cm: a virtual image on the object’s side (magnifying glass).

options.text_md: at F on the other side, real and point-sized
virtual, erect and enlarged
at infinity
at 2F on the other side, real, inverted and the same size

questions.solution_md: With $u = -2f$: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{2f} = \dfrac{1}{2f}$, so $v = 2f$ and $m = -1$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A plano-convex lens of glass (n = 1.5) has a curved surface of radius 15 cm. Find its focal length, in cm.
questions.solution_md: With $R_1 = +15$ cm and $R_2 = \infty$: $\dfrac{1}{f} = (1.5 - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{15} - 0\right) = \dfrac{1}{30}$, so $f = 30$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A biconcave lens of glass with n = 1.6 has both surfaces of radius 20 cm. Find its focal length, with sign, in cm (3 significant figures).

**Assertion (A):** A convex glass lens (n = 1.5) has a longer focal length when it is immersed in water than in air.

**Reason (R):** In water, the factor (n − 1) in the lens maker’s formula is replaced by (n_glass/n_water − 1), which is smaller.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; (1.5/1.33 − 1) ≈ 0.13 is much less than 0.5, so 1/f is smaller and f longer (about four times), as R explains — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A convex lens of power +4.0 D is in contact with a concave lens of power −2.5 D. Find the focal length of the combination, in cm (3 significant figures).
A point object in air is 40 cm in front of a CONCAVE spherical glass surface (n = 1.5) of radius 20 cm. Find the image distance v, with sign, in cm.
questions.solution_md: $R = -20$ cm (centre on the incident side). $\dfrac{1.5}{v} = \dfrac{1.5 - 1}{-20} + \dfrac{1}{-40} = -0.025 - 0.025 = -0.05$, so $v = -30$ cm: a virtual image in front of the surface.

questions.stem_md: A glass lens (n = 1.5) is immersed in a transparent liquid that also has refractive index 1.5. The lens

options.text_md: becomes a stronger converging lens
becomes a diverging lens
behaves like a flat sheet of glass: it neither converges nor diverges light
reflects all light that enters it

questions.solution_md: The relative index is 1, so (n_rel − 1) = 0 and 1/f = 0: no refraction at its surfaces — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A thin symmetric biconvex lens of focal length f is cut into two equal plano-convex halves by a plane perpendicular to its axis. The focal length of each half is

options.text_md: 2f
f
4f

questions.solution_md: For the whole lens $\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\dfrac{2}{R}$; each half has one curved face: $\dfrac{1}{f'} = (n - 1)\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2f}$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? If the lower half of a convex lens is covered with black paper, only the upper half of the image is formed.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Every part of the lens forms a complete image; covering half the lens lets through less light, so the full image is formed but is dimmer.

questions.stem_md: An object 2.0 cm tall stands 24 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 16 cm. Find the position, size and nature of the image.

answer.model_answer_md: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{16} - \dfrac{1}{24} = \dfrac{1}{48}$, so $v = 48$ cm (on the far side). $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{48}{-24} = -2.0$, so the image is $2 \times 2.0 = 4$ cm tall. It is **real, inverted and magnified** (the object is between F and 2F).

questions.solution_md: Lens formula, then m = v/u.

questions.stem_md: When a prism is set at the angle of minimum deviation,

options.text_md: the angle of incidence is zero
the ray inside the prism travels parallel to its base and i = e
the emergent ray grazes the second face
the deviation equals the prism angle

questions.solution_md: At minimum deviation the path is symmetric: r₁ = r₂ = A/2 and i = e — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A prism of angle 60° gives a minimum deviation of 40°. Find the refractive index of its glass (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{60 + 40}{2}}{\sin 30^\circ} = \dfrac{\sin 50^\circ}{0.5} \approx 1.53$.

questions.stem_md: A thin prism of angle 5.0° is made of glass of refractive index 1.5. The deviation it produces is about
questions.solution_md: For a thin prism $\delta \approx (n - 1)A = 0.5 \times 5.0 = 2.5^\circ$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For refraction through a prism of angle A, the angles of refraction at the two faces, r₁ and r₂, satisfy

options.text_md: r₁ − r₂ = A
r₁ + r₂ = A
r₁ + r₂ = 180° − A
r₁ = r₂ always

questions.solution_md: The normals to the two faces meet at an angle 180° − A, so in the triangle formed r₁ + r₂ = A — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A graph of deviation against angle of incidence for a prism is U-shaped. Explain why, apart from the minimum, each value of deviation occurs at two angles of incidence.

answer.model_answer_md: Light paths are **reversible**: a ray entering at angle i and leaving at e has the same deviation as one entering at e and leaving at i. So each deviation (except the minimum) occurs for **two** angles of incidence, i and e. At the minimum the two coincide (**i = e**), giving the single lowest point of the U.

questions.solution_md: Reversibility swaps i and e.

marking_scheme.step: Reversibility: i and e can be interchanged
They coincide only at minimum deviation

questions.stem_md: A prism of angle 60° has refractive index √2. Find its angle of minimum deviation and the angle of incidence at which it occurs.

answer.model_answer_md: At minimum deviation $r = A/2 = 30^\circ$, so $\sin i = n\sin r = \sqrt2 \times 0.5 = 0.707$ and $i = 45^\circ$. Then $\delta_m = 2i - A = 90^\circ - 60^\circ = 30^\circ$. (Check: $\sin\frac{60 + 30}{2}/\sin 30^\circ = \sqrt2$.)

questions.solution_md: r = A/2, Snell, δm = 2i − A.

questions.stem_md: The objective of a compound microscope has a very short focal length so that it

options.text_md: forms a large real image of a tiny object placed just outside its focus
forms a virtual image for the eyepiece
collects light from very distant objects
reduces the size of the image

questions.solution_md: With the object just beyond a short focus, v is large compared with |u|, giving a large linear magnification v/u — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 120 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 4.0 cm. Find its magnifying power in normal adjustment.
Find the magnifying power of a simple microscope of focal length 2.5 cm when the image is formed at the near point (D = 25 cm).
A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 0.50 cm, an eyepiece of focal length 2.5 cm and a tube length of 16 cm. Estimate its magnifying power with the final image at infinity.
questions.solution_md: $m \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e} = \dfrac{16}{0.50} \times \dfrac{25}{2.5} = 32 \times 10 = 320$.

questions.stem_md: A telescope with lenses of focal lengths 120 cm and 5.0 cm is set in normal adjustment. The distance between the lenses is

options.text_md: 125 cm
115 cm
24 cm
600 cm

questions.solution_md: In normal adjustment the image formed by the objective is at the focus of both lenses: L = fo + fe = 125 cm — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student looks through a telescope from the wrong end (through the objective). Distant objects now appear

options.text_md: smaller, with angular magnification fe/fo (less than 1)
larger, with magnification fo/fe
the same size
larger, with magnification fo + fe

questions.solution_md: The roles of the lenses swap: magnification becomes fe/fo < 1, so objects look smaller and farther away — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Astronomical telescopes are built with objectives of very large diameter mainly to

options.text_md: increase the magnifying power fo/fe
shorten the tube
collect more light and resolve finer detail
remove the need for an eyepiece

questions.solution_md: Light-gathering power grows with the area of the objective, and a wider aperture resolves closer stars; magnification depends on the focal lengths — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A reflecting telescope does not suffer from chromatic aberration.

**Reason (R):** A mirror reflects light of all wavelengths in the same way.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; since reflection does not depend on wavelength, all colours focus at the same point, which explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A simple microscope gives a larger magnifying power when the image is formed at the near point than when it is at infinity.

**Reason (R):** The near point of a normal eye is about 25 cm.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R alone does not explain A. A follows from m = 1 + D/f (near point) compared with m = D/f (infinity) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Why should both the objective and the eyepiece of a compound microscope have short focal lengths?

answer.model_answer_md: The magnifying power is about $\dfrac{L}{f_o}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e}$. A **short f_o** makes the objective’s image much larger than the object (large $L/f_o$), and a **short f_e** makes the eyepiece a stronger magnifier (large $D/f_e$). Both increase the total magnification.

questions.solution_md: m ∝ 1/(fo fe).

marking_scheme.step: Short fo and fe both increase m

questions.stem_md: Give two advantages of a reflecting telescope over a refracting telescope.

answer.model_answer_md: Any two: **no chromatic aberration** (mirrors reflect all colours alike); a **paraboloidal** mirror removes spherical aberration; a mirror can be **supported over its whole back**, so very large apertures are possible; a large mirror is **lighter and cheaper** than a lens of the same size.

questions.solution_md: List two.

questions.stem_md: A telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5.0 cm. Find its magnifying power (a) in normal adjustment, (b) when the final image is at the near point, 25 cm from the eye. (c) Which setting gives the larger magnification?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = \dfrac{100}{5.0} = 20$.
(b) $m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \dfrac{f_e}{D}\right) = 20 \times \left(1 + \dfrac{5.0}{25}\right) = 24$.
(c) The near-point setting gives the larger magnification (24 against 20), though normal adjustment is more comfortable for long viewing.

questions.solution_md: fo/fe; then multiply by (1 + fe/D).

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain total internal reflection and derive the relation between the critical angle and the refractive index for light going from a medium into air. (b) Explain how an optical fibre transmits light, and why its cladding has a lower refractive index than its core. (c) Find the critical angle for diamond (n = 2.42) and explain why diamonds sparkle.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) When light passes from a denser medium (index n) into air, it bends away from the normal. As i increases, r reaches 90° at the **critical angle** C; for larger i no light is refracted and all of it is reflected — **total internal reflection**. Snell’s law at the critical angle: $n\sin C = 1 \times \sin 90^\circ$, so $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n}$.

(b) A fibre has a thin glass **core** surrounded by **cladding** of lower index. Light entering near the axis meets the core–cladding boundary at more than the critical angle ($\sin C = n_\text{clad}/n_\text{core}$), so it is totally reflected again and again and travels along the fibre with little loss, even round gentle bends. The cladding must be optically **rarer** so that TIR can occur at the boundary (and it protects the core surface).

(c) $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{2.42} \approx 0.413$, so $C \approx 24.4^\circ$. With such a small critical angle, light entering a cut diamond is totally reflected many times at its faces and leaves mainly through the top, so the stone sparkles.

questions.solution_md: Snell at r = 90°; fibre by repeated TIR; small C for diamond.

marking_scheme.step: Fibre: repeated TIR at core–cladding boundary

questions.stem_md: (a) Using the formula for refraction at a spherical surface, derive the lens maker’s formula for a thin lens in air. (b) A biconvex lens of glass (n = 1.5) has radii of curvature 30 cm and 60 cm. Find its focal length and power. (c) What would happen to its focal length in a liquid of refractive index 1.5?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For the first surface (radius $R_1$), light goes from air ($n_1 = 1$) into glass ($n_2 = n$): $\dfrac{n}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{n - 1}{R_1}$. The image $I_1$ acts as the object for the second surface (radius $R_2$), from glass into air: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{n}{v_1} = \dfrac{1 - n}{R_2}$ (thin lens: distances measured from the same centre). Adding: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$. For an object at infinity $v = f$, so $\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$.

(b) $R_1 = +30$ cm, $R_2 = -60$ cm: $\dfrac{1}{f} = 0.5\left(\dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{60}\right) = 0.5 \times \dfrac{3}{60} = \dfrac{1}{40}$, so $f = 40$ cm and $P = \dfrac{1}{0.40} = 2.5$ D.

(c) The relative index becomes 1.5/1.5 = 1, so $1/f = 0$: the focal length becomes **infinite** and the lens has no focusing effect.

questions.solution_md: Two surfaces, add, set u = −∞.

marking_scheme.step: Second surface equation with I₁ as object

questions.stem_md: (a) Trace the path of a ray through a prism and show that r₁ + r₂ = A and δ = i + e − A. (b) Derive the relation for the refractive index in terms of A and the angle of minimum deviation. (c) A 60° prism gives a minimum deviation of 38°. Find its refractive index and the angle of incidence at minimum deviation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A ray enters face AB at incidence $i$, refracts at $r_1$, meets face AC at $r_2$ and emerges at $e$. The normals at the two faces meet at a point N; in quadrilateral A–(entry)–N–(exit) the angles at the faces are 90°, so the angle at N is $180^\circ - A$. In the triangle formed by the ray inside and the two normals, $r_1 + r_2 + (180^\circ - A) = 180^\circ$, so $r_1 + r_2 = A$. The deviations at the faces are $(i - r_1)$ and $(e - r_2)$, so $\delta = i + e - (r_1 + r_2) = i + e - A$.

(b) At minimum deviation $i = e$ and $r_1 = r_2 = r$. Then $2r = A$, $r = A/2$, and $\delta_m = 2i - A$, so $i = \dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}$. Snell’s law: $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$.

(c) $i = \dfrac{60 + 38}{2} = 49^\circ$; $n = \dfrac{\sin 49^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} \approx 1.51$.

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw (describe) the ray diagram of a compound microscope with the final image at the near point, and derive an expression for its magnifying power. (b) A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 2.0 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 6.25 cm. An object is placed 2.5 cm from the objective, and the final image is at 25 cm from the eye. Find the magnifying power.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The object is placed just outside the focus of the objective, which forms a real, inverted, enlarged image A′B′ just inside the focus of the eyepiece. The eyepiece acts as a simple microscope and forms a virtual, enlarged final image at the near point. Magnifying power $m = m_o \times m_e$, where $m_o = \dfrac{v_o}{u_o}$ (linear magnification by the objective) and $m_e = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}$ (eyepiece with image at D). So $m = \dfrac{v_o}{u_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$ (in magnitude).

(b) Objective: $\dfrac{1}{v_o} = \dfrac{1}{2.0} - \dfrac{1}{2.5} = \dfrac{1}{10}$, so $v_o = 10$ cm and $|m_o| = \dfrac{10}{2.5} = 4.000000000000001$. Eyepiece: $m_e = 1 + \dfrac{25}{6.25} = 5$. Total $|m| = 4 \times 5 = 20.000000000000004$.

questions.solution_md: m = m_o m_e; lens formula for the objective.

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw (describe) the ray diagram of an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment and derive its magnifying power. (b) A telescope has lenses of focal lengths 150 cm and 6.0 cm. Find its magnifying power and tube length in normal adjustment. (c) Describe a Cassegrain reflecting telescope and give one advantage over a refracting telescope.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Parallel rays from a distant object, at angle α to the axis, are focused by the objective to an image at its focus F_o, a distance $f_o$ from it. The eyepiece is placed so that this image is also at its focus, so the rays leave parallel at angle β (final image at infinity). If the image has height h: $\tan\alpha \approx \alpha = \dfrac{h}{f_o}$ and $\tan\beta \approx \beta = \dfrac{h}{f_e}$, so $m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}$.

(b) $m = \dfrac{150}{6.0} = 25$; tube length $= 150 + 6.0 = 156$ cm.

(c) A large **concave primary mirror** collects light and reflects it towards a small **convex secondary mirror**, which sends it back through a hole in the primary to the eyepiece or camera. Advantage: no chromatic aberration (also: large mirrors can be supported from behind and are cheaper).
